title: What causes `OOMKilled` even when monitoring looks normal (container memory limit vs JVM heap/off-heap, container-aware JVM flags), and how do you right-size requests/limits?
shortTitle: Why Pods Get OOMKilled Even When Monitoring Looks Normal, and Right-Sizing Requests/Limits

s1_definition.profdef: OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage exceeded the container's memory limit. It can happen even when heap dashboards look fine because the container limit caps total process memory, which includes the JVM heap plus off-heap memory such as thread stacks, metaspace, code cache, direct byte buffers, and native allocations. Right-sizing means setting the memory request to the typical working set and the limit above the real peak, and making the JVM container-aware so its heap sizing respects the cgroup limit rather than the whole node.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a teller's cubicle has a strict space limit for everything they bring in. Your dashboard only measures the papers on the desk (the JVM heap), but the cubicle limit counts the desk papers plus the filing cabinet, the chair, the coat rack, and the coffee machine (off-heap and native memory). So the cubicle can overflow and security evicts the teller even though the desk papers looked modest on the report. The fix is to measure the whole cubicle, not just the desk, and to tell the teller how big the cubicle actually is so they do not bring a desk sized for a whole floor.
s1_definition.oneliner: OOMKilled is the cgroup limit cap on TOTAL memory (heap plus off-heap plus native), not just the heap your dashboard shows, so size limits to real peak and make the JVM container-aware.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage exceeded the container's memory limit. It can happen even when heap dashboards look fine because the container limit caps total process memory, which includes the JVM heap plus off-heap memory such as thread stacks, metaspace, code cache, direct byte buffers, and native allocations. Right-sizing means setting the memory request to the typical working set and the limit above the real peak, and making the JVM container-aware so its heap sizing respects the cgroup limit rather than the whole node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a teller's cubicle has a strict space limit for everything they bring in. Your dashboard only measures the papers on the desk (the JVM heap), but the cubicle limit counts the desk papers plus the filing cabinet, the chair, the coat rack, and the coffee machine (off-heap and native memory). So the cubicle can overflow and security evicts the teller even though the desk papers looked modest on the report. The fix is to measure the whole cubicle, not just the desk, and to tell the teller how big the cubicle actually is so they do not bring a desk sized for a whole floor.

**One line to remember:** OOMKilled is the cgroup limit cap on TOTAL memory (heap plus off-heap plus native), not just the heap your dashboard shows, so size limits to real peak and make the JVM container-aware.

sections.s2_technical:
A container's memory limit is enforced by the Linux cgroup. When the sum of all memory the process touches crosses that limit, the kernel kills the process with signal 9 and Kubernetes records the container's last state as OOMKilled with exit code 137. The critical insight is what counts toward that limit: it is the entire resident memory of the JVM process, not just the Java heap. The heap is only one region. Off-heap and native memory also count, including thread stacks (each thread costs around half a megabyte to a megabyte), metaspace for class metadata, the JIT code cache, direct byte buffers used heavily by Netty and NIO, memory-mapped files, and native allocations by libraries.

This is exactly why monitoring can look normal. If your dashboard graphs only heap usage and the heap sits comfortably at sixty percent, you conclude everything is fine, but the container still gets OOMKilled because thread stacks, metaspace, and direct buffers pushed total resident memory past the limit. A thread leak that spawns thousands of threads, or a direct-buffer leak, will OOM-kill a container while the heap graph stays flat.

The JVM flags matter enormously. Older JVMs read the host machine's total memory, not the container limit, so inside a container with a one-gigabyte limit an old JVM might size its default heap for a thirty-two-gigabyte node and get killed immediately. Modern JVMs are container-aware by default, honoring the cgroup limit. I still set it explicitly with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, which tells the JVM to size the maximum heap as a percentage of the container limit, for example seventy-five percent, leaving the remaining quarter for off-heap and native memory. I avoid hardcoding `-Xmx` to a fixed value that ignores the limit, and I never set the heap equal to the whole container limit because that leaves nothing for the rest.

Right-sizing requests and limits is a measurement exercise. The request is what the scheduler reserves and should reflect the typical working set so Pods schedule sensibly; the limit is the hard cap and should sit above the observed real peak of total memory with some headroom. I measure actual usage under realistic load using container memory metrics, not just heap, then set the request near the steady state and the limit comfortably above the peak. I also understand QoS implications: when request equals limit the Pod is Guaranteed and is the last to be evicted under node pressure, whereas a Burstable Pod with request below limit is more exposed. For a banking service I lean toward Guaranteed memory for the critical path. The senior discipline is to profile native memory with Native Memory Tracking when heap looks innocent, because a flat heap graph combined with OOMKills almost always means an off-heap or native leak.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service kept getting OOMKilled in production while the heap dashboard showed a healthy sixty percent. The scenario reproduces the hidden-memory trap.

Problem 1 — the container limit was one gigabyte and we set the heap to nearly a gigabyte, leaving almost nothing for thread stacks, metaspace, and the direct buffers our HTTP client used. Under load, total memory crossed the limit and the container was OOMKilled with exit code 137, even though heap was fine. This is exactly the heap-versus-total confusion.

Problem 2 — an older base image used a JVM that sized the heap from the node's thirty-two gigabytes, ignoring the one-gigabyte limit, so the Pod died on startup. The fix was a container-aware JVM with MaxRAMPercentage.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `ContainerMemoryModel` that tracks heap plus off-heap plus native against a cgroup limit, an `OomKiller` that fires when total crosses the limit, and a `JvmSizer` that computes a safe max heap from the limit using a RAM percentage. We run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya under a badly-sized config (OOMKilled) and a right-sized config (succeeds), logging the breakdown.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the memory sizing simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/mem/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.mem.MemorySizingDemo

# Real cluster: confirm OOMKilled and inspect total (not just heap)
kubectl describe pod transfer-xyz | grep -A3 "Last State"   # Reason: OOMKilled, exit 137
kubectl top pod transfer-xyz                                 # container memory (total)
# Native Memory Tracking when heap looks innocent:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a one-gigabyte container limit, first with an oversized heap and then with a container-aware heap.

Step 1 — Under the bad config, the heap is set to 960 MiB. The dashboard would show only this heap and it looks reasonable against the limit. But the model adds metaspace of 96, thread stacks of 80, and direct buffers of 120, giving a total of 1256 MiB.

Step 2 — The OOM killer compares the total of 1256 MiB to the limit of 1024 MiB. The total exceeds the limit, so the kernel sends SIGKILL and the container is OOMKilled with exit code 137. The log stresses that the heap looked fine, which is the exact real-world confusion.

Step 3 — We switch to a container-aware configuration. The JvmSizer computes the max heap as seventy-five percent of the one-gigabyte limit, which is 768 MiB, deliberately leaving a quarter of the limit for off-heap and native memory.

Step 4 — The good model uses a heap of 768 MiB plus metaspace 96, thread stacks 80, and direct buffers 60, for a total of 1004 MiB, which is just under the 1024 MiB limit.

Step 5 — The OOM killer sees the total within the limit, so the container stays up. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully, proving that leaving headroom for off-heap memory prevents the kill while still using most of the limit for heap.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 00:59:40.100 [INFO] mem: heap=960 meta=96 stacks=80 direct=120 TOTAL=1256MiB / limit=1024MiB (dashboard shows only heap=960)
2026-10-30 00:59:40.101 [SEVERE] OOMKilled: total 1256MiB > limit 1024MiB — SIGKILL, exit code 137 (heap looked fine!)
2026-10-30 00:59:40.102 [INFO] transfer attempt under BAD sizing killed=true
2026-10-30 00:59:40.103 [INFO] JVM container-aware: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 on limit 1024MiB -> maxHeap=768MiB
2026-10-30 00:59:40.104 [INFO] mem: heap=768 meta=96 stacks=80 direct=60 TOTAL=1004MiB / limit=1024MiB (dashboard shows only heap=768)
2026-10-30 00:59:40.105 [INFO] memory within limit — container stays up
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage crossed the container's memory limit, and Kubernetes records that as exit code 137. The reason it can happen while monitoring looks perfectly normal is that most dashboards graph only the Java heap, but the container limit caps the entire resident memory of the process. That total includes the heap plus a lot of off-heap and native memory: thread stacks, metaspace for class metadata, the JIT code cache, direct byte buffers used heavily by networking libraries, memory-mapped files, and native allocations. So the heap can sit at a comfortable sixty percent while thread stacks and direct buffers quietly push the total past the limit and get the container killed.

The JVM flags are central to avoiding this. Older JVMs read the host machine's memory rather than the container limit, so inside a one-gigabyte container an old JVM might size its heap for a thirty-two-gigabyte node and die immediately. Modern JVMs are container-aware, and I make it explicit by setting the maximum heap as a percentage of the container limit, typically seventy-five percent, which deliberately leaves the remaining quarter for off-heap and native memory. I never set the heap equal to the whole limit, because that starves everything else and guarantees an OOM kill under load.

Right-sizing requests and limits is a measurement exercise rather than a guess. The request is what the scheduler reserves and should match the typical working set so Pods schedule sensibly, while the limit is the hard cap and should sit above the real observed peak of total memory with some headroom. I measure actual container memory under realistic load, not just heap, and for a critical banking path I often set request equal to limit so the Pod gets Guaranteed quality of service and is the last to be evicted under node pressure.

In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service kept getting OOMKilled while the heap dashboard showed a healthy sixty percent. The cause was that we had sized the heap at nearly the full one-gigabyte limit, leaving no room for thread stacks, metaspace, and the direct buffers our HTTP client allocated, so total memory crossed the limit even though heap looked fine. Setting the heap to seventy-five percent of the limit with a container-aware flag, graphing the container's total working set instead of just the heap, and using Native Memory Tracking to confirm there was no native leak, eliminated the kills while still using most of the limit productively.
